requirements.statement: The Approval Service holds approval authority under an OS principal independent of the AI agent. The agent-side client can only submit a request and read its status; it cannot approve, modify the trusted plan, sign, read keys or the ledger, or reach privileged operations, and without verified isolation the service and client fail closed.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: The IPC protocol has no approve or sign message; approval happens only through the operator channel.
The service refuses to start in production when its protected storage, configuration or executable are writable by any non-service principal, and reports isolation honestly in health.

The client treats the service as isolated only when the endpoint owner differs from its own identity and the service attests verified isolation in a production build; otherwise it reports unisolated and refuses protected writes.
Keys, ledger, configuration and audit live outside any user repository; logs never contain tokens or credentials.

requirements.statement: A human approves or rejects the exact operation through WebAuthn (Touch ID, Windows Hello, FIDO2) on a page rendered from the service's own canonical plan, never from agent-supplied text; the challenge binds the exact plan, any material change invalidates the approval, and production accepts no machine approval.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: The page shows work item, repository, provider and instance, action type, exact target, branch and revision, files or commit summary, remote destination, plan fingerprint, expiry, material risks and reversibility, all derived by the service from the repository.
Signature, origin, RP ID, credential, challenge and user verification are verified; the challenge is the hash of the exact decision and is single use.
A plan changed after it was shown is not approved; an approval is never reused for another action, repository, revision or request.
A production build refuses the machine channel; a development build labels it as test-only.

requirements.statement: A trusted Executor inside the service performs the approved git_commit, git_push and git_merge_request itself, after independently re-deriving and validating the scope, with TOCTOU protection, replay idempotency and honest reporting of what the boundary can and cannot guarantee (credential separation for push, unrestricted agent write access for local commits). Provider execution for Jira uses the same protocol through strict provider interfaces.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: Exact repository, remote, branch, refs, revision and file hashes are bound; a mismatch at execution is refused before the approval is consumed; commit uses plumbing with a compare-and-swap ref update and never runs repository hooks.

Git is run with argument arrays only, a sanitized environment, service-owned configuration and credentials, and refuses repositories whose local configuration can execute code or redirect credentials.
Replay returns the recorded result; failures report whether anything changed and how to roll back; no credential or token is returned to the agent.

The executor and plan documents state which guarantees hold (push with credentials the agent does not hold) and which cannot (agent can still commit locally); merge and release stay separate capabilities.

requirements.statement: The service is cross-platform: a platform-independent core (protocol, plans, WebAuthn, executor, ledger, audit) and thin adapters for macOS (launchd daemon, pkg), Windows (service) and Linux (systemd), distributed with Praxis with minimal setup. A platform is claimed secure only after its trust boundary has been tested on that OS; each platform's status is reported separately and honestly.

acceptanceCriteria.statement: The core has no dependency on launchd, Keychain or other platform APIs; adapters supply paths, endpoint, isolation probe and install/uninstall plans.

macOS: a built installer package, an unprivileged dry-run of the install plan, uninstall, upgrade and migration procedures; the privileged installation is presented to the owner and not executed by the agent.
Windows and Linux: adapters and installer artifacts are generated and statically tested, and are labelled untested until built and run on those operating systems.

The Runtime client and praxis_doctor report service health, version, compatibility and isolation; installing the .mcpb alone never claims OS-level isolation; no approval material is ever written to a user repository.

decisionRecords.statement: One cross-platform Approval Service (Node, bundled, own runtime copy) owns broker and executor under a dedicated OS principal. Components: Runtime Client (in the Runtime, no secrets, IPC only), Service core (request state machine, canonical plan derivation from the repository, WebAuthn operator page reused from tools/broker, Ed25519-signed approval records, replay ledger, hash-chained audit), Trusted Executor (git commit via plumbing with compare-and-swap ref update and no hooks; push with service-owned credentials; merge request through the provider interface), and Platform adapters (paths, endpoint, isolation probe, install/uninstall plans) for macOS launchd, Windows service and Linux systemd. IPC is newline-delimited JSON over a local socket/pipe with no approve or sign message. Approval exists only through the operator channel (WebAuthn user-verified assertion over a challenge hashing the exact decision). A repository must be allow-listed in root-owned service configuration. The service fails closed in production when isolation checks fail; a development mode exists only in non-production builds and is reported as unisolated.
decisionRecords.rationale: Reuses the hardened broker pieces (authorizeGitOperation, operator-web, WebAuthn, authorization signing, assessor) instead of rewriting them, and moves execution out of the agent's process so push can use credentials the agent never holds. Threat model: assets are signing key, ledger, credentials, repository integrity, operator authenticators; attackers are the AI agent and any process running as the user. In scope: forging or replaying approvals, plan look-alikes, TOCTOU file/ref swaps, hook and config execution through the repository, credential redirection, path/symlink substitution, socket impersonation, log leakage. Out of scope and stated: a compromised administrator or kernel, an agent that already has the user's Git credentials, an agent that commits locally without the service (commit cannot be exclusive), enrollment abuse by someone with admin rights, malicious virtual authenticators if enrollment is not admin-gated (enrollment code is root-only).

stories.narrative: As a repository owner, I want to approve or reject exactly the Git operation an AI agent asks for, so that nothing is committed, pushed or opened for review without my decision.
stories.objective: The owner sees the operation the service derived from the repository and decides; the service then acts once, or not at all.
stories.userValue: The owner keeps control of what leaves the repository without having to read the agent's own description of it.
preconditions: The Approval Service is running and an authenticator is enrolled
The agent has submitted a commit request for named files
happyPath: The agent submits the request
The service shows the owner the files, branch, revision and remote it derived
The owner approves with a user-verified authenticator
The service creates one commit with exactly those files
negative: Executing before a decision is refused
edgeCases: The owner approves, then a file changes before execution: the approval does not cover the new content
businessRules: One approval authorizes one operation on one request

acceptanceCriteria.when: the owner approves and the agent asks for execution
acceptanceCriteria.then: exactly one commit is created, authored by the service, containing exactly the named files
the repository, remote and index are unchanged and execution is refused

acceptanceCriteria.given: a real Touch ID or security key
acceptanceCriteria.when: the owner approves on the operator page
acceptanceCriteria.then: the assertion is verified with user verification and the approval is accepted (needs the owner)

stories.narrative: As a repository owner, I want the AI agent to be unable to approve its own requests or bypass the service, so that an approval means a person decided.
stories.objective: The agent can only ask and read status; forged, replayed or machine approvals, unknown operations and an absent or unverified service never result in a protected operation.
stories.userValue: The approval is meaningful even when the agent is hostile or confused.
preconditions: The agent can write to the repository and connect to the service socket
happyPath: The agent sends approve, sign, enroll and configuration messages
The service refuses each as an unknown operation
The agent plants a token signed by another key or with a machine channel
Execution is refused and nothing changes
negative: A service that is missing, speaks another protocol or cannot show isolation makes the client refuse
A production service whose isolation checks fail does not start
edgeCases: An agent-owned process claims production isolation on its own socket
businessRules: Isolation is judged from ownership evidence, never from what the service says about itself

acceptanceCriteria.when: any message other than submit, status, execute or health is sent
acceptanceCriteria.then: it is refused as UNKNOWN_OPERATION and extra fields are refused

acceptanceCriteria.when: a token signed by another key or on the machine channel is planted
acceptanceCriteria.then: execution is refused and the repository is unchanged

acceptanceCriteria.given: an absent, impostor or unverified service or a missing trust anchor
acceptanceCriteria.then: it fails closed with nothing changed

expectedResults: No path from the agent to an approval

stories.actor: AI agent acting for the repository owner
stories.narrative: As a requesting agent, I want to ask again for an operation that already completed and get the recorded result, so that a retry never repeats a commit, push or review request.
stories.objective: One execution id is bound to one request and one set of parameters; asking again returns what happened even after the repository and remote moved on.
stories.userValue: Retries after a timeout or restart are safe, and a changed request cannot ride on an old approval.
preconditions: A commit, a push and a merge request were each approved and executed
happyPath: The repository HEAD and the remote branch have moved on
The agent asks again with the same execution id
The service returns the recorded result and runs nothing
negative: The same execution id with a different message, path, branch or remote is refused as a changed plan
edgeCases: The file changes between approval and execution: the approval is refused before it is consumed
businessRules: A failed execution that changed nothing may be asked for again with a fresh approval; an uncertain one may not

acceptanceCriteria.given: completed commit, push and merge request
acceptanceCriteria.when: each is requested again with its execution id after HEAD and the remote moved
acceptanceCriteria.then: each returns its recorded result and nothing runs a second time

acceptanceCriteria.when: the request differs in any bound parameter or the content changes after approval
acceptanceCriteria.then: it is refused and nothing changes

stories.narrative: As a repository owner, I want approval keys and credentials and the ledger and configuration to stay out of the agent's reach and out of my repositories, so that the agent cannot forge or reuse an approval or leak a credential.
stories.objective: Secrets never appear in replies, logs or repositories; no approval branches or files are created; protected data is unreadable and unwritable by the agent's OS identity.
stories.userValue: Approval material cannot be stolen or planted by the agent.
preconditions: The service runs as its own OS principal (needs installation)
happyPath: A full commit flow runs
No token, key or credential appears in any reply or log
No branch, ref or file for approvals appears in the repository
negative: As the agent's OS user, reading the key, listing state, appending the audit log, writing the ledger or configuration, replacing the code or socket, signalling or reading the service process are all denied
businessRules: Independence from the agent is a property of the OS identity, not of the code; it is proven only where the service actually ran as another principal

acceptanceCriteria.when: replies, audit log and the repository are inspected
acceptanceCriteria.then: no token or key appears and the repository gained no approval refs or files

acceptanceCriteria.given: the service running as its own OS principal
acceptanceCriteria.when: the agent's user attempts to read or modify protected data or the service
acceptanceCriteria.then: every attempt is denied (verified on Linux in a container; macOS and Windows need the owner)

stories.narrative: As a repository owner, I want the service to detect tampering with its own records and to survive restarts and concurrent requests, so that a rolled-back log or ledger cannot make a consumed approval usable again.
stories.objective: Truncated or rolled-back audit and ledger are detected and refused; restarts recover; concurrent requests stay isolated.
stories.userValue: The record of what was approved can be trusted after crashes and attacks.

history.note: Praxis must ship an Approval Service that runs under an isolated OS identity on macOS, Windows and Linux, presents the exact operation to a human who approves with WebAuthn (Touch ID, Windows Hello, FIDO2), and executes approved Git operations (commit, push, merge request) itself, so the AI agent can only request and read status. Platform adapters isolate the OS-specific parts; macOS is implemented and tested first, Windows and Linux are reported separately and honestly.
